name: Radio-frequency skin tightening

card.summary: A non-surgical procedure that heats the deeper skin with radio-frequency energy to tighten lax skin and soften wrinkles for a firmer jawline and face.
card.note: Done by clinicians with cleared devices; burns, uneven healing and dents are reported with improper use.

quick.overview:
Radio-frequency (RF) skin tightening uses high-frequency electrical energy to warm the dermis, the deeper layer of skin, without breaking the surface. The heat makes collagen fibers contract and prompts new collagen to form over the following months, which is meant to firm sagging skin along the jowls, neck, eyes and body and smooth fine lines.

It is positioned as a non-surgical option between doing nothing and a facelift. Published studies, including reviews and clinical series, report improvements in laxity, and combination RF treatments have been evaluated for lower face and neck laxity.
quick.how: Treatments are performed in a clinic with a device using monopolar, bipolar or microneedle RF electrodes, often with surface cooling. Some protocols use one session and others a series. Results develop gradually over months as collagen remodels. Handheld at-home RF devices also exist.
quick.risks: Reported effects include redness, pain and swelling that resolve within days. Wikipedia notes that some patients had pain severe enough to need sedation, that improper application can leave dents from uneven healing, and that fat necrosis and atrophic scarring have been reported. Burns and pigment changes can occur with misuse, particularly with microneedling variants.

lead: Radio-frequency skin tightening is a non-surgical aesthetic procedure that uses radio-frequency energy to heat the skin so that collagen, elastin and hyaluronic acid production is stimulated and fine lines and loose skin are reduced [1]. People use it to firm sagging skin on the jowls, neck, eye area, abdomen, thighs and arms, and it is presented as an alternative to a facelift [1].

Devices differ by electrode design: monopolar, bipolar and unipolar systems penetrate to different depths, and microneedle variants deliver RF into the dermis [1]. A dermal temperature of about 67 degrees Celsius is considered ideal for remodeling, according to Wikipedia [1]. Well-known systems include Thermage from Solta Medical, Venus Concept's devices, Syneron's VelaShape and BTL's Exilis [1].

Research includes a 2011 review in Clinics in Plastic Surgery describing RF as the mainstay of non-invasive skin tightening [2], a retrospective review of combined bipolar and fractional RF for lower face and neck laxity [3], and a study of a multi-source RF protocol for full-face rejuvenation [4]. Controlled trials are registered for monopolar RF for facial wrinkles [5].

chain: Collagen contracts and new collagen forms
Firmer skin, tighter jawline and smoother lines
angle.text: RF tightening is used to firm mild to moderate laxity in the jawline, neck and eye area without surgery. Results build over several months as collagen remodels.

paras: RF devices pass alternating current through the skin, and tissue resistance converts it to heat that tightens collagen fibers and triggers remodeling [1]. By adjusting surface cooling, RF can also be used to heat tissue in order to reduce fat [1]. Common treatment areas include jowls, abdomen, thighs and arms [1].

Uses include tightening lax skin, reducing wrinkles, improving cellulite and body contouring [1]. A surgical review notes a 'treatment gap' of patients not severe enough for excisional surgery but beyond what traditional non-invasive options address, which combination RF is used to fill [3]. Energy-based devices including RF are also discussed for skin of color [6].

Wikipedia reports that some patients experienced pain severe enough to require sedation, that improper application can cause dents from uneven healing, and that fat necrosis and atrophic scarring have been reported [1]. Research on monopolar RF over dermal fillers in an animal model examined how RF affects filler substances [7].

A 2011 review of non-invasive and minimally invasive RF skin tightening focused on peer-reviewed articles and technologies with the most proven or promising results, describing RF as the mainstay of non-invasive tightening [2]. A retrospective review of combined bipolar RF (FaceTite) and fractional bipolar RF for lower face and neck laxity was described as the largest evaluation of such combinations to date [3]. A study of a multi-source RF protocol combining tightening, fractional resurfacing and microneedle RF assessed safety and efficacy for full-face rejuvenation [4]. Registered trials include a monopolar device study for facial wrinkles with 284 participants [5] and a bipolar RF microneedling study of submental laxity [8]. Wikipedia also lists a 2010 randomized comparison of fractional RF with surgical facelift and a 2018 trial of microneedle RF for cellulite [1].
